# CPU scheduling from the administrator view: priorities and affinity

After reading this page, you will be able to read and set nice values within unprivileged limits, inspect scheduling policy with `chrt`, pin a process to CPU lists with `taskset`, and decide when affinity helps isolation versus when it creates artificial bottlenecks.

## What an administrator controls

The kernel's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) decides which `SCHED_OTHER` task runs next. You rarely tune CFS knobs on a production host. You *do* adjust:

1. **Nice** — a relative priority hint among ordinary tasks.
2. **CPU affinity** — which CPUs a task may run on.
3. **Real-time policies** (`SCHED_FIFO` / `SCHED_RR`) — privileged; mentioned here so you recognize them, not so you enable them casually.

Deep scheduler implementation belongs in a later performance track. This page stays at the admin tools you already have on a stock Linux host.

## Nice and priority

Nice ranges from `-20` (most favored) to `19` (least favored). Ordinary users may **raise** nice (make a task less urgent) but cannot lower it without privilege. `ps` shows `NI` (nice) and `PRI` (a derived priority column; higher `PRI` here means less favored under the `ps` display used below).

```bash
sleep 30 &
SP=$!
ps -o pid,ni,pri,psr,cmd -p $SP

nice -n 10 sleep 30 &
SP2=$!
ps -o pid,ni,pri,psr,cmd -p $SP2
kill $SP $SP2 2>/dev/null
```

Verified on an 8-CPU host running Linux 6.12:

```text
    PID  NI PRI PSR CMD
2254557   0  19   3 sleep 30
    PID  NI PRI PSR CMD
2254560  10   9   3 sleep 30
```

The second `sleep` runs at nice `10`. Batch jobs, backups, and compile farms are good nice candidates; latency-critical request handlers usually stay at nice `0`.

### Unprivileged attempts to raise priority fail

```bash
nice -n -5 true
```

Verified message:

```text
nice: cannot set niceness: Permission denied
```

GNU `nice` still runs the command at the current nice when the adjustment is denied. Check `$?` and the message; do not assume the negative nice took effect. Permanent lower nice values need capabilities, sudo rules, or a systemd unit with `Nice=` under a privileged service context.

`renice` adjusts an already-running PID:

```bash
renice -n 15 -p PID
```

Same privilege rules apply.

## Inspecting policy with `chrt`

```bash
sleep 30 &
SP=$!
chrt -p $SP
kill $SP
```

Typical ordinary task:

```text
pid 2254562's current scheduling policy: SCHED_OTHER
pid 2254562's current scheduling priority: 0
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Not run here.** Setting `SCHED_FIFO` / `SCHED_RR` with `chrt -f` / `chrt -r` requires privilege and can starve the rest of the system if misused. Prefer documenting the policy you *observe* on vendor realtime services over enabling RT for ordinary apps.
:::

## CPU affinity with `taskset`

Affinity restricts the CPUs on which a task may be scheduled. Use it to keep a noisy worker off a latency-sensitive core, or to match a NIC's IRQ placement — not as a substitute for fixing an overloaded service.

```bash
taskset -c 0 sleep 30 &
SP3=$!
sleep 0.2
taskset -p $SP3
ps -o pid,ni,psr,cmd -p $SP3
grep -E '^(Name|State|Cpus_allowed_list):' /proc/$SP3/status
kill $SP3
```

Verified output:

```text
pid 2254562's current affinity mask: 1
    PID  NI PSR CMD
2254562   0   0 sleep 30
Name:	sleep
State:	S (sleeping)
Cpus_allowed_list:	0
```

Mask `1` means CPU 0 only (`1 << 0`). `PSR` shows the CPU the task last ran on — here `0`, matching the mask. `Cpus_allowed_list` is the durable view under `/proc`.

Useful forms:

| Command | Meaning |
| :--- | :--- |
| `taskset -c 0,2 CMD` | Run `CMD` only on CPUs 0 and 2 |
| `taskset -c 0-3 CMD` | CPUs 0 through 3 |
| `taskset -p MASK PID` | Show or set mask on an existing PID |
| `taskset -cp LIST PID` | Set with a CPU list instead of a hex mask |

systemd units can set `CPUAffinity=` so the service starts already pinned; prefer the unit over ad-hoc `taskset` when the workload is managed by systemd.

## When affinity helps — and when it hurts

**Helps** when you isolate a latency path from a bulk worker, when hardware locality matters (NUMA-aware placement in a later part), or when reproducing a bug that only appears on a single CPU.

**Hurts** when you pin a multi-threaded server to one core and create artificial contention, or when you shrink the allowed set so far that CFS has no idle CPU left for that task while other cores sit empty.

Measure before and after: wall time, run-queue latency (`perf sched` / `schedstat` in deeper tooling), and application SLOs. Affinity without a measurement story is cargo-cult tuning.

## Common mistakes

- Treating `PRI` from `ps` as a knob you set directly — change nice or policy instead.
- Pinning everything to CPU 0 "for consistency" and then wondering why that core saturates.
- Assuming negative nice worked after a permission error.
- Jumping to realtime priorities for a slow Python service — fix the code path first.


## systemd unit knobs (preview)

When the workload is a service, prefer unit directives over one-off shell wrappers:

| Directive | Role |
| :--- | :--- |
| `Nice=` | Static nice for the service processes |
| `CPUAffinity=` | Allowed CPU list |
| `CPUWeight=` / `CPUQuota=` | cgroup CPU shares and quota (deeper in later Part 07 briefs) |

::: {.callout-note}
**Not run here.** Editing system units and reloading systemd needs administrative access. Read the directives from `man systemd.exec` and apply them in a lab VM when you have one.
:::

Affinity in a unit survives restarts; a manual `taskset -p` on a live PID is wiped when the service forks a replacement process unless the manager reapplies it.

## Reading load versus pressure

High load average with low application throughput can mean runnable tasks waiting on CPU (`R` state pile-up) or tasks blocked on I/O (`D`). Nice and affinity only help the CPU-runnable case. Pressure stall information (PSI) and cgroup CPU accounting appear later in Part 07; use them before pinning random processes to CPU 0.

### Quick evidence loop

```bash
nproc
ps -eo pid,ni,psr,pcpu,cmd --sort=-pcpu | head
grep Cpus_allowed_list /proc/$(pgrep -n sleep)/status 2>/dev/null || true
```

Sort by `%CPU`, note `PSR` scatter, then decide whether a batch job at nice 10 would protect interactive work — often yes — or whether the hot process is already the interactive one (affinity will not invent spare cores).


## Summary

For ordinary workloads, nice and affinity are the safe admin levers. Raise nice on batch work, pin only with a reason and a measurement, and treat realtime policies as privileged exceptions. Read `NI`, `PSR`, `chrt -p`, and `Cpus_allowed_list` so scheduling stories stay grounded in evidence.
